look_here_first: KNOTGRASS / WETLAND PASPALUM: often TWO narrow one-sided V-shaped flowering racemes, but that alone is not a species ID. It spreads in wet ground by surface STOLONS that root at nodes. The original photo proves the two-raceme V; the NEW licensed meadow photo shows low mat-like habit but does NOT prove individual rooted nodes. Separate from P. notatum (bahia grass) with a true runner and mature spikelet anatomy.

crew_field_steps: Photograph the two seedhead branches from their common point; the existing image unmistakably shows a pair of spreading reproductive racemes.
Zoom into each one-sided spikelet row and distinguish green spikelets from the dark protruding anthers and stigmas.
Photograph a REAL stolon with roots coming from a node in moist ground; none of the present project photos shows the rooted habit.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole plant patch and creeping stolon rooting at nodes on moist soil.
Head photographed straight on from branching joint, showing the paired racemes.
Face-on two rows of spikelets along a raceme with mm scale.
Close blade/sheath collar and a mature spikelet for P. notatum discrimination.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Search actual growing horizontal stems and root-bearing nodes, rather than interpreting two racemes alone. Bahia grass P. notatum also often makes two racemes; grass-root habit and mature upper-glume/spikelet measurements must corroborate. The Australian wetland image is not proof of Texas nativity.
do_not_use_alone: Number of racemes without the entire flowering axis
Habitat, height, or vegetative tuft in isolation
Microscopic glume hairs or spikelet length inferred from a photo without scale
comparisons.field_identification_note: Pair the two-raceme photo with a legal close field photo exposing a rooted aboveground stolon node and centimeter ruler. Photograph complete leaf collar and a ripened spikelet; preserve geography and nativity uncertainty.

visual_comparison.title: Paspalum distichum — photographed field ID and look-alikes
visual_comparison.subtitle: Photos already in the Hays library, inspected individually. Annotations point ONLY to visible shapes/parts; small hairs/glumes and exact species determinations await specimen proof.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: COUNT COMPLETE RACEMES → MEASURE 5 RIPE SPIKELETS → CHECK MARGINAL HAIRS → ROOTED BASE/COLLAR. DALLIS few large silky; VASEY many small silky; FLORIDA few big round; PUBIFLORUM smaller oval; SETACEUM narrow variable; DISTICHUM two + real stolons.

items.caption: This is Paspalum setaceum according to its existing source photo, NOT Paspalum distichum. Compare the pictured flowering architecture or plant habit; different frames are not measured side-by-side specimens.
items.why_it_matters: Knotgrass combines wet-ground creeping stolons with usually paired (rarely three) unilateral flowering racemes. Bahia grass can produce two racemes but differs in low turf/rhizome architecture and spikelet structure. Thin paspalum may form just one or a few flowering branches but has different leafy habit and varietal hair traits; Florida paspalum forms robust upright bunches and bigger oval spikelets.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Paspalum: what to inspect
steps: Pair the two-raceme photo with a legal close field photo exposing a rooted aboveground stolon node and centimeter ruler. Photograph complete leaf collar and a ripened spikelet; preserve geography and nativity uncertainty.
First show the WHOLE head, then ONE one-sided raceme and attached spikelets. Never treat a photograph of one branch as total raceme count.
Obtain a real intact mature spikelet and measure it with 1-mm reference; use margin hair pattern and glumes to separate close Paspalum taxa.
Photograph blade/sheath joint and same-plant rootstock; knotgrass needs actually rooted horizontal stolons, not merely a low mat.
If plant photo is source-labelled only, keep identity tentative and leave existing county-native fields unchanged.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Knotgrass combines wet-ground creeping stolons with usually paired (rarely three) unilateral flowering racemes. Bahia grass can produce two racemes but differs in low turf/rhizome architecture and spikelet structure. Thin paspalum may form just one or a few flowering branches but has different leafy habit and varietal hair traits; Florida paspalum forms robust upright bunches and bigger oval spikelets.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Gross photo structures are references, NOT expert confirmation. Even new licensed images are PROVISIONAL — USER PHOTO REVIEW PENDING and not proof of Hays County presence.
